cards.title: Social Spending Across Rich Countries
cards.definition: The most direct way to compare the size of welfare states is public social spending: what general government pays out for social purposes such as pensions, health, and income support, measured as a share of GDP. The measure has limits. It leaves out private social spending, mainly health insurance and pensions, and it does not show how much of a benefit is taxed back, so countries with similar public spending can differ in what households actually receive.
cards.example: In the OECD Social Expenditure Database, public social spending averaged 20 percent of GDP in 2019, rose to 23 percent in 2020 mostly because spending jumped during the pandemic, then fell to 22.1 percent in 2021 and an estimated 20.5 percent in 2022. In 2024 it was highest, at just over 30 percent of GDP, in Austria, Finland, and France, and 15 percent or less in Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ireland, Mexico, and Türkiye. Private social spending added about 3.5 percent of GDP on average in 2021, and 12.8 percent in the United States.

cards.title: The Earned Income Tax Credit
cards.definition: Some welfare programs pay support only to people who work. The U.S. Earned Income Tax Credit is delivered through the income tax, and its amount depends on earned income, adjusted gross income, filing status, and the number of qualifying children. Earned income means pay from a job or from self-employment; unemployment benefits, Social Security benefits, pensions, interest, and dividends do not count. A household with no earnings from work therefore cannot receive the credit, which ties this form of support to work.

Eligibility ends at adjusted gross income limits that rise with family size: $19,104 for a single filer with no children and $61,555 with 3 or more, and $26,214 and $68,675 for married couples filing jointly. cards.title: Pension Replacement Rates
cards.definition: A replacement rate compares a retiree's pension with what the same person earned while working. The net version takes account of the income taxes and social security contributions paid on both, so it reflects disposable income before and after retirement; on average it is higher than the gross version because workers pay higher effective tax and contribution rates on earnings than retirees pay on pensions. Many pension systems give low earners a higher replacement rate than high earners.
cards.example: The OECD's Pensions at a Glance 2025 calculates with its pension models that for an average earner with a full career, the net replacement rate from mandatory pension schemes at the normal retirement age averages 63.2 percent across OECD countries, 11.2 percentage points above the gross rate. It ranges from under 35 percent in Ireland and Lithuania to 85 percent or more in 7 countries, including the Netherlands, Portugal, and Spain. For low earners, on half of average earnings, the average is 75.2 percent; for high earners, on twice average earnings, 52.9 percent.

cards.title: Who Receives Cash Benefits
cards.definition: Welfare states can direct cash to the poorest through income tests, or tie benefits to past earnings through social insurance. The two designs spread money differently. Income-tested benefits concentrate payments on low-income households, while earnings-related benefits pay more to people who earned and contributed more. As a result, a country can spend heavily on cash transfers yet send a relatively small share of them to its lowest-income households. Neither pattern alone shows which design is better; they pursue different goals.
cards.example: In 2020, the OECD found, only 23 percent of the public cash transfers received by working-age people went to households in the poorest fifth of the income distribution on average, while 20 percent went to the richest fifth. More than 40 percent went to the poorest fifth in Australia, Finland, and the Netherlands, which use various income-tested benefits. Less than 15 percent did in Greece, Italy, Luxembourg, Portugal, Spain, and Türkiye, where social insurance is strong and most benefits are related to past earnings.

cards.title: Withholding
cards.definition: Withholding is income tax taken out of each paycheck by the employer and sent to the government on the worker's behalf. It is a prepayment, not the final bill. How much is withheld depends on two things: how much the worker earns and the information the worker gives the employer on Form W-4. Employers are required by law to withhold, and the same rule applies to Social Security and Medicare taxes. Tax can also be withheld from pensions, bonuses, and commissions.
cards.example: A worker paid every 2 weeks receives 26 paychecks a year, and each one carries a slice of the year's expected income tax. If the total withheld over the year is more than the tax actually owed on the return, the difference comes back as a refund; if it is less, the worker owes the balance at filing time. The IRS offers an online estimator to check the setting during the year.

cards.title: Form W-4
cards.definition: Form W-4, the Employee's Withholding Certificate, is the form a worker gives an employer so that the right amount of federal income tax is withheld. It tells the employer about filing status, other jobs in the household, dependents, and any extra amount to withhold per paycheck. It is not filed with a tax return; the employer keeps it. The IRS suggests reviewing it each year and whenever circumstances change, because the form only reflects what the worker last reported.
cards.example: Two common triggers are a marriage and a second job. A couple who both work and each file a W-4 as married filing jointly without completing Step 2, for multiple jobs or a working spouse, can end up under-withheld, because each employer assumes its paycheck is the household's only income. Filing a new W-4 after the change corrects the estimate for the remaining paychecks of the year.

cards.title: Form W-2
cards.definition: Form W-2, the Wage and Tax Statement, is the employer's annual report of what it paid an employee and what it withheld. Copies go to the worker and to the government, so the numbers on a return can be matched against the employer's report.

If an employer discovers an error after issuing the form, it files a corrected statement, Form W-2c, so that the worker's record and the return can be matched. A missing form is requested from the employer first.

cards.title: Payroll Taxes: Social Security and Medicare
cards.definition: Alongside income tax, paychecks carry payroll taxes under the Federal Insurance Contributions Act. Two separate taxes apply: one funds Social Security's old-age, survivors, and disability insurance and one funds Medicare's hospital insurance. Each is paid half by the employee and half by the employer, at flat rates. Only the Social Security portion has a wage base limit, an annual ceiling on earnings subject to the tax; Medicare tax applies to all covered wages, with an additional rate above a high threshold.
cards.example: The rates published by the IRS are 6.2 percent each for employee and employer for Social Security, 12.4 percent combined, and 1.45 percent each for Medicare, 2.9 percent combined. For earnings in 2026 the Social Security wage base limit is $184,500. An Additional Medicare Tax of 0.9 percent is withheld on wages above $200,000 in a calendar year, with no employer match.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Filing Status
cards.definition: Filing status is the category a taxpayer files under, and it sets the standard deduction, the bracket thresholds, and eligibility for some credits. The IRS lists five: single; married filing jointly; married filing separately; head of household; and qualifying surviving spouse. Status is generally determined by marital situation on the last day of the year, so a December wedding counts for the whole year. When more than one status fits, the taxpayer may choose the one that produces the lower tax.
cards.example: Head of household is for an unmarried person who paid more than half the cost of keeping up a home for themselves and a qualifying dependent; it carries a larger standard deduction than single. Qualifying surviving spouse applies for up to 2 years after a spouse's death when there is a dependent child. The IRS notes that most married couples pay less by filing jointly than separately.

cards.title: Tax Brackets Are Marginal
cards.definition: Federal income tax is charged in layers called brackets. Each bracket's rate applies only to the slice of taxable income that falls inside it, not to the whole amount. Moving into a higher bracket therefore raises the tax on the next dollar earned, not on the dollars already taxed at lower rates. The rate on the last dollar is the marginal rate; total tax divided by total income is the average rate, and once income reaches a second bracket the average rate is lower than the marginal rate.
cards.example: For tax year 2025 a single filer's first $11,925 of taxable income is taxed at 10 percent, the next slice up to $48,475 at 12 percent, and the slice up to $103,350 at 22 percent. An illustrative single filer with $60,000 of taxable income owes $1,192.50 plus $4,386 plus $2,535.50, about $8,114 in total: a 22 percent marginal rate but an average rate near 13.5 percent.

cards.title: Refunds and Balances Due
cards.definition: A refund is not a bonus; it is the return of tax that was prepaid through withholding or estimated payments beyond what the year's return shows is owed. A balance due is the reverse. Both are settled when the return is filed. Refunds can be reduced to pay past-due federal taxes, child support, or certain other debts before the remainder is sent, and returns that claim some credits are held by law until mid-February so the claims can be checked.
cards.example: The IRS describes typical timing: about 3 weeks after an electronically filed return and 6 or more weeks after a mailed one, with delays when a return needs correction or review. Refund status can be checked 24 hours after e-filing a current-year return, or 4 weeks after mailing a paper return. A large refund every year means more was withheld than needed all year long.

cards.title: Self-Employment Tax
cards.definition: Someone who works for themselves has no employer to withhold tax or to pay the employer half of Social Security and Medicare. Self-employment tax fills that gap: it is both halves combined, calculated on net earnings using Schedule SE and paid with the return, usually through quarterly estimated payments. Because an employee never sees the employer share, the combined rate looks large by comparison. The law offsets part of it by letting the self-employed deduct the employer-equivalent half when computing adjusted gross income.
cards.example: The self-employment tax rate is 15.3 percent: 12.4 percent for Social Security plus 2.9 percent for Medicare. It applies once net self-employment earnings reach $400 or more in a year. Only earnings up to the annual Social Security wage base, a limit shared with any wages from a job, are subject to the Social Security part, while the Medicare part applies to all of them, with an extra 0.9 percent above a filing-status threshold.

cards.title: Form 1099-NEC
cards.definition: Form 1099-NEC, Nonemployee Compensation, is the information return a business files to report pay for services from someone who is not its employee, such as an independent contractor. It plays the role a W-2 plays for an employee, but it reports a different kind of worker. The IRS instructions note that amounts reported this way to individuals are generally subject to self-employment tax, which the person paid works out and pays.
cards.example: For tax years beginning after 2025 the reporting threshold rose to $2,000: a business files Form 1099-NEC for each person it paid at least $2,000 for services during the year. The test is applied payer by payer, so an illustrative designer paid $1,500 by one client and $2,500 by another in 2026 would receive a form from the second client only.

cards.title: Estimated Tax Payments
cards.definition: Federal income tax is meant to be paid as income is earned. Wages have tax withheld, but income such as self-employment earnings, interest, dividends, or capital gains may have none, so the tax is prepaid through estimated payments instead. For this purpose the IRS divides the year into 4 payment periods, each with its own due date, and paying too little by a period's due date can bring a penalty even when the return later shows a refund.
cards.example: For tax year 2026, Publication 505 sets the due dates at April 15, June 15, and September 15, 2026, with the payment for September through December due January 15 of the following year. The periods are not equal: January to March covers 3 months, April and May only 2, June to August 3, and September to December 4. A due date that falls on a weekend or legal holiday moves to the next business day.

cards.title: Why W-2 Boxes 1 and 3 Differ
cards.definition: A W-2 reports wages more than once because each tax uses its own definition. Box 1 holds the wages counted for federal income tax, Box 3 the wages subject to Social Security tax, and Box 5 the wages subject to Medicare tax. Elective deferrals to a traditional 401(k) plan are left out of Box 1 but still counted in Boxes 3 and 5, and the amount deferred is listed separately in Box 12 with code D.
cards.example: The 2026 W-2 instructions limit Boxes 3 and 7 together to $184,500, the Social Security wage base, and show an employee paid $199,750 with $184,500 in Box 3 and $199,750 in Box 5, which has no limit. An illustrative worker earning $70,000 who defers $5,000 to a traditional 401(k), with no other pre-tax deductions, would see $65,000 in Box 1 but $70,000 in Boxes 3 and 5.

cards.title: The Estimated Tax Safe Harbor
cards.definition: An individual generally has to make estimated tax payments only when two things are both true: the tax still owed after withholding and refundable credits is expected to be at least $1,000, and withholding and refundable credits are expected to fall short of the smaller of 90 percent of the current year's tax or 100 percent of the tax on the prior year's return. The prior-year test becomes 110 percent when the prior year's adjusted gross income was above $150,000, or $75,000 for married filing separately.
cards.example: An illustrative filer had $8,000 of total tax on the prior year's return and expects $12,000 for the current year. Ninety percent of $12,000 is $10,800, so the smaller target is the prior year's $8,000; with prior-year adjusted gross income above $150,000 it becomes 110 percent, or $8,800. Withholding that reaches the target meets the test even though at least $3,200 would still be owed when the return is filed.

topics.name: Buying a Car or a Home
topics.summary: How auto loans, leases, and mortgages are priced and disclosed, and the mechanics of negative equity, down payments, PMI, points, title insurance, the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure, escrow, and home equity.

cards.title: Reading the Loan Disclosure
cards.definition: Before an auto loan is signed, the federal Truth in Lending Act requires the lender or dealer to hand over a disclosure that states the loan's cost in a standard way. Four numbers matter most: the annual percentage rate, which folds interest and mandatory fees into one yearly percentage; the finance charge, the total interest and fees over the life of the loan; the amount financed; and the total of payments. The monthly payment alone hides the last three.
cards.example: An illustrative $25,000 loan at a 7 percent rate costs about $599 a month over 48 months, a finance charge near $3,735 and a total of payments around $28,735. The same loan stretched to 72 months costs about $426 a month - but the finance charge rises to roughly $5,688 and the total to about $30,688. Each disclosure states those totals in writing; a quoted monthly payment alone does not.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Leasing Versus Buying
cards.definition: A lease buys the right to use a car for a set time and a set number of miles; a loan buys the car. Lease payments are usually lower than loan payments on the same vehicle because the lessee pays only for the depreciation expected during the term, plus a rent charge, taxes, and fees, and hands the car back at the end unless the contract allows a purchase. The lessee also carries obligations a buyer does not: mileage caps, wear standards, and early-termination charges.
cards.example: The FTC notes that most standard leases cap mileage at 15,000 a year or less; a higher cap raises the payment because the car loses more value, and exceeding it brings an added fee at return. Someone who drives 20,000 miles a year and keeps cars for 8 years faces very different costs under the two contracts, even when the first year’s payments look similar.

cards.title: Negative Equity
cards.definition: Negative equity means owing more on a car loan than the car is worth. It arises because a new car loses value quickly while a long loan pays down principal slowly, and it grows with small down payments and rolled-in fees. It surfaces at trade-in time: a dealer may offer to fold the shortfall into the next loan, which raises the new balance, lengthens the term, or increases the payment, and starts the next loan already underwater.
cards.example: An illustrative driver owes $18,000 on a car worth $15,000 as a trade-in: $3,000 of negative equity. Rolling it into a $25,000 purchase means financing $28,000 for a car worth $25,000 on day 1. The CFPB's guidance is to learn the loan's payoff amount, which can differ from the statement balance, and to confirm about a week after the new deal that the old loan was actually paid off.

cards.title: Fixed and Adjustable Mortgages
cards.definition: A fixed-rate mortgage keeps the same interest rate, and therefore the same principal-and-interest payment, for the life of the loan. An adjustable-rate mortgage starts with a rate that holds for an introductory period and then resets at regular intervals. The new rate is an index - a broad measure of market interest rates - plus a margin the lender sets, subject to caps that limit how far the rate can move at each reset and over the loan's life.
cards.example: Suppose an illustrative adjustable loan starts at 5 percent for 5 years with a margin of 2.5 percentage points. If the index stands at 4 percent at the first reset, the new rate is 6.5 percent - unless a cap limits the jump. The CFPB cautions against assuming a sale or refinance will come before the reset, since home values and personal finances can change.

cards.title: Down Payments and PMI
cards.definition: The down payment is the part of the price paid in cash; the mortgage covers the rest. The ratio between them changes the loan's terms. On a conventional loan with less than 20 percent down, lenders generally require private mortgage insurance, a policy the borrower pays for but that protects the lender if payments stop. PMI is charged as a monthly premium, an up-front premium at closing, or both, and it appears on the Loan Estimate and the Closing Disclosure.
cards.example: On an illustrative $300,000 home, 10 percent down is $30,000 and leaves a $270,000 loan that would ordinarily carry PMI; 20 percent down is $60,000 and a $240,000 loan without it. The CFPB notes that some lenders offer low-down-payment loans without PMI in exchange for a higher interest rate, which can cost more or less than PMI depending on how long the borrower keeps the loan.

cards.title: The Loan Estimate
cards.definition: The Loan Estimate is a standardized 3-page form a mortgage lender must deliver within 3 business days of receiving an application. Every lender uses the same layout, which is the point: it lets a borrower line up offers from different lenders and compare the interest rate, monthly payment, estimated taxes and insurance, and total closing costs. It also flags features worth knowing about, such as a prepayment penalty or negative amortization. Receiving one does not mean the loan is approved.
cards.example: A borrower who applies to 3 lenders on the same day can expect 3 Loan Estimates by the end of the third business day and can compare them page by page. Closing costs include lender fees, third-party charges, and prepaid items such as property taxes and homeowners insurance. The form shows what the lender expects to offer; the final figures arrive on the Closing Disclosure.

cards.title: Escrow Accounts
cards.definition: An escrow account, called an impound account in some states, is a holding account the mortgage servicer runs to pay property taxes and insurance premiums on the borrower's behalf. A share of each monthly payment goes into it, and the servicer pays the bills when they fall due, once or twice a year. Many lenders require escrow so that the taxes and insurance protecting their collateral are certain to be paid. Because those bills change, the escrow portion of the payment is recalculated each year.
cards.example: If an illustrative home carries $3,600 a year in property taxes and $1,200 in homeowners insurance, the escrow share of the payment is $400 a month on top of principal and interest. A borrower without escrow must set that $4,800 aside alone. The CFPB warns that if taxes or insurance go unpaid, the lender may buy force-placed insurance, typically more expensive, and bill the borrower.

cards.title: Home Equity
cards.definition: Home equity is the home's market value minus what is still owed on the mortgage. It grows two ways: as payments reduce the loan balance and as the home's price rises. Early payments are mostly interest, so the first route is slow at first, and the second can run in reverse when prices fall. Selling also costs money, so after a short stay the transaction costs can leave an owner with no more equity than at purchase.
cards.example: An illustrative buyer puts $30,000 down on a $300,000 home. If the price stays flat, 3 years of payments on the 30-year, $270,000 loan at 6.5 percent cut the balance by about $9,700; selling costs of $10,000 would leave about $29,700, slightly less than was put in. The CFPB notes that when prices fell between 2007 and 2012, many owners lost some or all of their equity.

cards.title: Title Insurance
cards.definition: Title is legal ownership of a home, and the deed shows that the seller passed it to the buyer. Title insurance covers the risk that someone later claims a right to the home that arose before the purchase, such as a claim from a previous owner's unpaid taxes or from a contractor who says a past job was never paid for. The policy most lenders require protects the amount they lend; a separate owner's policy protects the buyer's own investment.
cards.example: A buyer can face 2 title policies at closing: the lender's policy, which most lenders require, and an owner's policy, which the buyer decides whether to buy. The CFPB notes that title insurance can usually be shopped for separately from the mortgage, and that buying both policies from 1 provider usually costs less in total. An itemized title charge at closing can differ from the Loan Estimate or Closing Disclosure without necessarily meaning the charge is wrong.

cards.title: The Closing Disclosure
cards.definition: The Closing Disclosure is the form that gives the final details of a mortgage: the loan terms, the projected monthly payments, and the fees and other costs of getting the loan, known as closing costs. The lender must provide it at least 3 business days before closing. That window exists so the borrower can compare the final terms and costs with the Loan Estimate received earlier and ask the lender questions before signing.
cards.example: The Closing Disclosure runs 5 pages. Not every home loan uses it: a reverse mortgage borrower instead receives 2 forms, a HUD-1 settlement statement and a final Truth-in-Lending disclosure, and someone taking out a home equity line of credit receives neither a HUD-1 nor a Closing Disclosure but should receive a Truth-in-Lending disclosure.

cards.title: Discount Points and Lender Credits
cards.definition: Points and lender credits trade cash at closing against the interest rate. One point equals 1 percent of the loan amount, paid at closing for a lower rate than the same lender's zero-point loan; a lender credit works in reverse, lowering closing costs in exchange for a higher rate. Points are listed on page 2, Section A of the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure, and credits appear as a negative number in the Lender Credits line of Section J.
cards.example: In the CFPB's example, a $180,000, 30-year fixed loan is offered at 5.0 percent with no points. Paying 0.375 points, or $675, lowers the rate to 4.875 percent and the payment by about $14 a month; accepting a $675 credit instead raises the rate to 5.125 percent and the payment by about $14. Dividing $675 by $14 gives roughly 48 months, about 4 years of lower payments to recover the points, ignoring what the cash could earn elsewhere.

cards.title: When the Three-Day Clock Restarts
cards.definition: Under Regulation Z, the Closing Disclosure must reach the borrower no later than the third business day before closing, and for this rule a business day is every calendar day except Sundays and federal legal public holidays. If terms change before closing, a corrected form usually only has to arrive at or before closing. Just 3 changes require a new 3-business-day wait: the annual percentage rate becomes inaccurate, the loan product changes, or a prepayment penalty is added.
cards.example: Because Saturdays count, a disclosure handed over in person on a Friday allows closing on the following Tuesday, absent a holiday: Saturday, Monday, and Tuesday are the 3 business days. In the rule's official commentary, for a regular mortgage an APR disclosed at 7.00 percent that ends at 7.10 percent is still accurate and does not delay closing, while 7.15 percent is inaccurate and does. A mailed disclosure is treated as received 3 business days after it is mailed.

topics.summary: What builds a credit score, how to read and correct a credit report, how card billing disputes and loss limits work, how identity theft, phishing, and imposter scams work, and what regulators report about fraud losses.

cards.title: What Moves a Score
cards.definition: A credit score is a prediction of repayment built from a credit report, and each scoring model weighs a handful of behaviors. Payment history counts most: paying every account on time as agreed. Next is utilization, how much of available credit is in use; models read balances near the limit as strain. Length of history helps because it gives the model more evidence. Recent applications for new credit count against a score because they can signal financial trouble.
cards.example: The CFPB relays a common guideline: keep balances at no more than 30 percent of total credit limits. Closing 2 unused cards can therefore lower a score if the same balances now sit on 1 card near its limit. Carrying a balance on a card is not required for a good score, and paying in full each month avoids interest charges.

cards.title: Free Credit Reports

Federal law gives everyone the right to a free copy of their report from each of the 3 nationwide credit reporting companies once every 12 months, obtained through the single official website or phone line set up for that purpose. Additional free reports are available after a denial of credit, insurance, or employment based on a report.
cards.example: Beyond the free copy the law guarantees every 12 months, the 3 nationwide credit reporting companies have permanently extended a program that offers each report free once a week through the official website set up for free reports. A denial notice gives 60 days to request an additional free report from the company named in it.

cards.title: Disputing an Error
cards.definition: Errors in a credit report can lower a score and raise borrowing costs, and federal law gives the consumer a right to dispute them. A dispute goes to the credit reporting company - online, by phone, or by mail with copies of supporting documents - and often also to the company that supplied the information, called the furnisher. The reporting company must investigate, forward the dispute and evidence to the furnisher, and report the result back; it may decline only disputes it reasonably finds frivolous.
cards.example: The CFPB's checklist for a mailed dispute: full contact information, each item in question with its account number, a clear explanation of why it is wrong, a request to remove or correct it, a copy of the report page with the items circled, and copies - never originals - of documents. The same letter can go to all 3 companies if all 3 show the error, and certified mail with a return receipt creates a dated record.

cards.title: How Long Information Stays
cards.definition: Credit reporting companies may report most negative information for a limited time, after which it must drop off the report even though the company may keep it on file. Positive information can stay longer, and an on-time history can remain after an account is closed, which helps scores that reward long histories. No one can lawfully remove accurate negative information early; companies that charge fees to 'repair' credit can do nothing a consumer cannot do alone for free, which is to dispute actual errors.
cards.example: The general limit is 7 years for late payments and most other negative items, and up to 10 years for bankruptcies; a judgment can stay 7 years or until the statute of limitations runs out, whichever is longer. The limits do not apply when a report is used for a job paying more than $75,000 a year or for credit or life insurance above $150,000.

cards.title: Identity Theft
cards.definition: Identity theft is the use of someone's personal or financial information - a Social Security number, a card or account number, a date of birth - without permission, usually to open accounts, file claims, or make purchases in their name. The information is taken in mundane ways: a stolen wallet, discarded statements, card skimmers on pumps and machines, phishing messages, public Wi-Fi, and details posted on social media. The victim often learns of it only from the aftermath.
cards.example: Warning signs USAGov lists include debt-collection calls for accounts never opened, unfamiliar accounts on a credit report, and mail that stops arriving. Recovery runs through the FTC's identity theft site and the 3 credit reporting companies, where fraud alerts and a freeze can be placed. Someone whose information was used to file a false tax return completes IRS Form 14039, an affidavit that invalidates the fraudulent return.

cards.title: Credit Freezes and Fraud Alerts
cards.definition: A credit freeze locks a credit file so that no new credit account can be opened in the person's name - including by the person - until the freeze is temporarily lifted. It is free, does not affect scores, and can be placed by anyone at any time. A fraud alert is lighter: it leaves the file visible but tells lenders to verify identity before granting new credit. Freezes must be placed with each reporting company; an alert placed with one is passed to the others.
cards.example: The FTC describes 3 kinds of alert. An initial fraud alert lasts 1 year and can be renewed by anyone who suspects identity theft. An extended alert lasts 7 years, requires an identity theft or police report, and removes the person from prescreened credit and insurance offers for 5 years. An active-duty alert for servicemembers removes them from those lists for 2 years.

cards.title: Imposter Scams and Fraud Losses
cards.definition: An imposter scam is fraud by impersonation: the caller, texter, or emailer claims to be a government agency, a bank, a utility, a familiar company, or a relative in trouble, and uses that borrowed authority to extract money or personal information. The FTC collects fraud reports from consumers nationwide and publishes the totals each year. Reported losses understate the real figure, since many victims never report, but the pattern across categories and payment methods is informative.
cards.example: For 2025 the FTC reported $15.9 billion in fraud losses from 3 million fraud reports, up from 2.6 million reports and more than $12 billion in losses the year before. Imposter scams were the most frequently reported fraud, with more than 1 million reports and more than $3.5 billion lost. Investment scams cost the most, $7.9 billion.

cards.title: Ponzi Schemes
cards.definition: A Ponzi scheme is an investment fraud that pays earlier participants with money collected from later ones, while claiming the payments are returns on a real strategy. Little or nothing is actually invested, so the scheme depends on a constant inflow of new money; it collapses when recruiting slows or many participants try to withdraw at once. The warning signs the SEC lists match the mechanism: unusually steady returns in all market conditions, unregistered investments, unlicensed sellers, and strategies too secret or complex to explain.
cards.example: The name comes from Charles Ponzi, who took in investors in the 1920s with a postage-stamp arbitrage story. The SEC's Office of Investor Education notes that promoters often push participants to roll over rather than cash out by offering still higher returns for staying in, and that trouble receiving payments or errors on account statements are signs that funds are not being invested as promised.

cards.title: Phishing
cards.definition: Phishing is an email or text message made to look as if it came from a trusted source, such as a bank, a card issuer, a utility, or an online payment app, so that the reader clicks a link, opens an attachment, or gives up passwords, account numbers, or a Social Security number. The FTC notes that the messages often tell a story: suspicious log-in attempts, a problem with a payment, an unfamiliar invoice, a government refund, or a free coupon.
cards.example: The FTC's sample fake email has a generic greeting, says the account is on hold over a billing problem, and offers a link to update payment details, something the FTC says legitimate companies do not send by email or text. Phishing texts can be forwarded to 7726 (SPAM), phishing emails to the Anti-Phishing Working Group, and both reported to the FTC through ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

cards.title: Credit Card Billing Disputes
cards.definition: The Fair Credit Billing Act sets a dispute process for billing errors on credit cards and other revolving accounts; it does not cover loans such as personal loans or car loans. Billing errors include unauthorized charges, charges with the wrong date or amount, goods not accepted or not delivered as agreed, and payments not credited. The dispute goes in writing to the issuer's address for billing inquiries, and during the investigation the disputed amount and related finance charges may be withheld.
cards.example: The letter must reach the issuer within 60 days after the first bill showing the error was sent. The issuer then has 30 days to acknowledge it in writing, unless the problem is already resolved, and 90 days to resolve it. While it investigates, the issuer cannot report the disputed amount as delinquent or close the account over it, and an issuer that skips the procedure forfeits up to $50 of what it could collect, even if the bill was correct.

cards.title: Lost Cards: Credit Versus Debit
cards.definition: Federal law limits what a cardholder pays for use of a lost or stolen card without permission, but the limit depends on the kind of card and on timing. A credit card carries a flat cap. An ATM or debit card carries a sliding scale set by how quickly the loss is reported, which matters because a debit card takes money from the account right away. For both kinds, charges made after the loss is reported are not the cardholder's responsibility.
cards.example: The FTC summarizes the limits this way. A credit card used after it is lost costs the cardholder at most $50. For an ATM or debit card, reporting before any use means $0; reporting within 2 business days of learning of the loss means up to $50; later, but within 60 calendar days after the statement is sent, up to $500. After 60 days the loss can be all the money taken and possibly more, including money in linked accounts.

cards.title: Synthetic Identity Fraud
cards.definition: Synthetic identity fraud invents a person who does not exist. Real identifying details, often a Social Security number, are combined with made-up ones such as a phone number or email address, so no single real person's full identity is taken over. That separates it from ordinary identity theft and lets it go unnoticed for years: children's Social Security numbers are often used because the owners may not apply for credit or a job until much later.
cards.example: The Boston Fed's August 23, 2022 account of how one is built: a first credit application under the synthetic identity is often rejected because no history exists, but the attempt leaves the credit bureaus with a file for it. The fraudster keeps applying until approved, builds a positive payment record, and works toward higher credit limits and more products, so there is more to steal. The Federal Reserve began working with the payments industry on the problem in 2018.

topics.name: Compounding & Time
topics.summary: How interest is earned, compared, and annualized, why compounding rewards time, how present value runs it in reverse, what inflation does to real growth, and how to size savings in months rather than dollars.

cards.title: Principal and Interest
cards.definition: Principal is the money deposited or borrowed; interest is the price paid for its use, expressed as a percentage of principal per year. On a deposit, the bank pays the saver; on a loan, the borrower pays the lender. Simple interest is computed on the original principal only, so each period earns the same amount. Compound interest is computed on principal plus interest already credited, so each period's earnings are slightly larger than the last. Over long spans the difference becomes large.
cards.example: Under simple interest an illustrative $1,000 at 4 percent earns $40 every year - $400 after 10 years. Under annual compounding the same deposit earns $40 the first year, then $41.60 on $1,040, and so on, reaching about $480 of interest after 10 years. The FDIC's primer puts it plainly: the interest is added to the principal, and the next interest is earned on the new, larger principal.

cards.title: Regular Deposits Over Time
cards.definition: Compounding also works on money added along the way. Each deposit starts earning interest once it is in the account, so a steady monthly amount builds a balance with two parts: the deposits themselves and the interest they have earned. Deposits made early have the longest to compound, so the interest share of the balance keeps growing the longer the schedule runs. The SEC's compound interest calculator asks for the same inputs: a starting amount, a monthly contribution, a number of years, a rate, and how often interest compounds.
cards.example: An illustrative $100 a month at 5 percent a year, compounded monthly, grows to about $15,500 after 10 years, of which $12,000 is deposits and about $3,500 is interest. After 30 years the balance is about $83,200 on $36,000 of deposits, so interest makes up more than half of it. The rate is an assumption; real returns vary from year to year.

cards.title: A Guaranteed Doubling
cards.definition: A Series EE savings bond is a U.S. Treasury bond that earns a fixed rate of interest for up to 30 years. Treasury adds one promise on top of the rate: the bond will double in value 20 years after purchase, and if the fixed rate has not done that by then, Treasury adds the difference at 20 years. Because the guarantee arrives only at that date, how long the bond is held matters as much as the rate printed on it.
cards.example: EE bonds issued from May 1 to October 31, 2026 earn a fixed 2.40 percent. At that rate alone, $1,000 would grow to only about $1,600 in 20 years, so Treasury makes up the rest to bring it to $2,000. Doubling in 20 years works out to roughly 3.5 percent a year, paid in full only to an owner who waits the whole 20 years.

cards.title: APY: Comparing Rates Fairly
cards.definition: Two accounts can quote the same interest rate and pay different amounts, because one compounds more often. The annual percentage yield, or APY, removes that ambiguity: it is the total interest an account pays over a 365-day year, including the effect of compounding frequency, expressed as a single percentage of the deposit. Federal disclosure rules require banks to state it, so APY - not the nominal rate - is the number that makes savings accounts and certificates of deposit comparable.
cards.example: The rule's own worked example: an account that pays $53.90 of interest in a year on a $1,000 deposit, compounded daily, has an APY of 5.39 percent. By the same arithmetic, an illustrative 4 percent rate compounded monthly yields about 4.07 percent, and compounded daily about 4.08 percent - small gaps on one deposit, but the fair way to rank offers.

cards.title: The Rule of 72
cards.definition: The Rule of 72 is a mental shortcut for compounding: dividing 72 by an annual growth rate gives the approximate number of years for an amount to double. It is an approximation, most accurate for rates near 8 percent; it slightly overstates the doubling time at lower rates and understates it at higher ones. It works in reverse too: dividing 72 by an inflation rate gives roughly how long until money buys half as much. It assumes a constant rate, which real returns rarely deliver.
cards.example: The SEC's classroom material uses 9 percent: 72 divided by 9 is 8, so a sum growing at 9 percent doubles in about 8 years, and the exact answer is also 8.0. At 2 percent the rule gives 36 years against an exact 35. At an illustrative 24 percent - a common credit card rate - the rule says 3 years while the true doubling time is about 3.2, close enough to show how fast a carried balance grows.

cards.title: Savings Measured in Months
cards.definition: A cash reserve can also be measured in time rather than dollars: how many months of essential spending it would cover if income stopped. Measured that way, the target scales automatically with a household's costs, and it can be built in steps. The CFPB's guidance ties the amount to the person's own history of unexpected expenses and income swings rather than to a universal figure, and notes that a reserve of any size shortens recovery from a shock and reduces reliance on borrowing.
cards.example: For an illustrative household spending $2,400 a month on essentials, 3 months of runway is $7,200 and 6 months is $14,400. Saving $200 a month reaches the 3-month mark in 36 months; adding part of a tax refund, one of the strategies the CFPB describes, shortens that. The unit is months of time bought, which is why the same dollar total means different things to different households.

cards.title: Time in the Account
cards.definition: Because compounding accelerates, the length of time money stays on deposit matters more than most people expect, and it matters more than modest differences in rate. Two deposits of the same size at the same rate end up far apart if one is left three times as long. The FDIC's primer names the two variables together - the interest rate and time - as the pair that determines how much a balance grows, and it is the second that a saver controls most directly.
cards.example: An illustrative $1,000 at 5 percent a year grows to about $1,629 after 10 years and to about $4,322 after 30. The second 20 years add roughly $2,693 - more than 4 times what the first 10 added - even though the rate never changed. A saver who starts 10 years later and stops at the same date forgoes that later, largest stretch of growth.

cards.title: The National Deposit Rate
cards.definition: The FDIC publishes a national deposit rate for common account types: the average rate paid by insured banks and credit unions for which data is available, weighted by each institution's share of domestic deposits. It is a benchmark for what typical balances earn, not an offer from any institution. Set against inflation, it gives a rough real return - the deposit rate minus the inflation rate - which is negative whenever prices rise faster than the balance grows.
cards.example: As of August 17, 2026 the FDIC's national deposit rate was 0.38 percent for savings accounts, 0.63 percent for money market accounts, and 1.71 percent for 12-month certificates of deposit. Against an illustrative 3 percent inflation rate, a savings balance earning 0.38 percent loses about 2.5 percent of its purchasing power in a year, while the 12-month certificate loses about 1.3 percent.

cards.title: Present Value
cards.definition: Present value is what an amount due in the future is worth as of an earlier date. It is found by discounting: reducing the future amount by an interest rate for each period of waiting. The Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation uses present value to put a single figure on pension benefits that will be paid over future years.
cards.example: An illustrative $1,000 due in 5 years, discounted at 4 percent a year, has a present value of about $821.93, because $821.93 growing at 4 percent a year for 5 years reaches $1,000. Discounted at a higher rate, the same future $1,000 is worth less now; at a lower rate, more. Present value is compound growth run in reverse.

cards.title: Real Growth of Savings
cards.definition: The real growth of a balance is its gain in purchasing power: divide the balance's growth factor by the price level's growth factor over the same period, then subtract 1. Subtracting the inflation rate from the growth rate is a shortcut. When prices are rising, the shortcut lands further from zero than the exact figure, overstating a real gain and exaggerating a real loss, and the gap widens as inflation over the period grows.
cards.example: The seasonally adjusted CPI-U index rose from 271.903 in July 2021 to 332.813 in July 2026, an increase of 22.4 percent. An illustrative $10,000 growing 2 percent a year over those 5 years reaches about $11,041, up 10.4 percent. Dividing 1.104 by 1.224 gives a real loss of about 9.8 percent, leaving about $9,020 in July 2021 dollars; subtraction would put the loss at 12.0 percent.

cards.title: Annualizing a Return
cards.definition: Interest earned over a term shorter or longer than a year has to be annualized before it can be set against a yearly rate. The annual percentage yield formula in Regulation DD does it with compounding: add 1 to the interest divided by the principal, raise the result to the power of 365 divided by the days in the term, and subtract 1. Scaling the return to a year without compounding understates that figure for terms under a year and overstates it for longer terms.
cards.example: The regulation's own examples: $30.37 of interest on a $1,000 certificate of deposit over 182 days works out to an annual percentage yield of 6.18 percent, while scaling the 182-day return to 365 days without compounding gives about 6.09 percent. A 2-year certificate paying $133.13 in total has an annual percentage yield of 6.45 percent, below the 6.66 percent found by splitting the total return evenly over 2 years.

cards.title: Present Value of a Payment Stream
cards.definition: A pension or any other series of future payments can be given a single present value by discounting each payment for its own waiting time and adding the results. Payments further away are discounted more, so they count for less. The PBGC's definition adds a second adjustment: each amount is also weighted by the probability that it will be paid, which is why ongoing pension plans can build in assumptions such as an expected age at death.
cards.example: Three illustrative payments of $1,000, due in 1, 2, and 3 years and discounted at 5 percent, are worth about $952.38, $907.03, and $863.84 now: $2,723.25 in total, against $3,000 paid out. If each payment has only a 90 percent chance of being made, the present value falls to about $2,450.92. A higher discount rate or a lower probability shrinks the single figure further.
